result.summary: Checked the file's claim to hold, verbatim, every AC and AU control statement [source text withheld from the public copy] PDF fetched from nvlpubs.nist.gov has exactly the recorded SHA-256 and size (6,073,678 bytes; server Last-Modified 9 Dec 2020), so the source is unchanged. I extracted it with pdftotext -layout, parsed all 216 AC/AU controls and enhancements, and compared each of the file's 215 entries after normalization; boundaries were cross-checked with a second extractor (pdfminer), page images, Appendix C and NIST's CPRT data. Of 220 items tested, 212 are confirmed: 210 entries (183 statements identical word for word, line breaks included; 27 withdrawn entries correctly flagged) plus hash and size. Eight problems: withdrawn base control AC-13 is missing; AC-19(3), withdrawn in the source, shows the title fragment "IDENTIFIABLE OWNER" as its statement; AU-6(8), AU-6(9), AU-9(7) and AU-12(4) have truncated titles whose last words head the statement; the stated counts are wrong (source: AC 25 base, 147 in all, total 216, not 24/146/215); and the marker "[WITHDRAWN in Rev. 5]" sits on 17 controls already withdrawn in Rev. 4 (interpretive). No entry is foreign to the source. Caveat: the PDF is the December 2020 edition; NIST's current Release 5.2.0 (CPRT) words seven of these statements differently: AC-2(2), AC-2(7), AC-4(25), AC-9(2), AC-24, AU-2, AU-5(4).

problems.source_text: In many situations, using a weighted average method on the metric scores could provide an adequate indication for the CAC. However, there may well be cases when weighted minimum or maximum values might be more suitable. For example, the MC axis contains metrics for perception and tactical behavior. A low score for the perception capabilities for a UMS implies that it may not be able to support a high-level, complex, autonomous mission behavior. In this situation, the lower score between the perception and tactical behavior should be used as the requirement instead of the average.
problems.note: A negative search claim, not a quotation, and the source contradicts it. The same volume names 'weighted minimum' as an aggregation and gives a worked case in which the lower score governs 'instead of the average'. The passage is hedged ('may well be cases', 'might be more suitable') and concerns metric scores on the MC axis, so it does not make weakest-link a general NIST rule; but 'none found', 'The only partial support is (a)...(b)' and 'appears nowhere' are not true of the text. Related: section 2.4, p. 25, lists 'insufficient capability in any of the RACs' as a contributor to (lack of) safety. In Vol II the string 'minim' occurs 8 times; 'weakest' and 'bottleneck' occur 0 times in both volumes. This bears directly on the file's instruction to label belief #1 CONJECTURE and to stop citing ALFUS for it.

The Notes also shorten 6.2 d to 'a desktop computer running software', dropping the limit 'that is irrelevant to UMS operations' (the full item is quoted correctly at line 191). Interpretive, but it feeds the file's first-ranked recommendation.

result.summary: I tested the NIST requirements file (auditonomous origin/main; the same blob is on the roadmap branch) against the four documents it names, downloaded today from [source text withheld from the public copy], AI 100-1 and SP 800-53 Rev. 5. Titles, numbers, versions, dates and the stated page counts (47 and 73) match, and the one hash the file records (Volume I) is identical. I tested 122 items: 4 document descriptions, the 20 requirements, 64 further quotations and fragments, 18 counts, 14 negative or paraphrase claims and 2 not-obtained statements. 109 were confirmed, 12 have problems (11 entries) and 1 could not be checked. All 20 requirement quotations are in the named document and section and every definitional label holds; 17 are fully confirmed. NIST-R15 drops a sentence without an ellipsis, and NIST-R9 and NIST-R18 cite a page one too low. The most serious problem is a negative claim: the file says neither ALFUS volume has a minimum or weakest-link formulation, but Volume II section 6.1 (page 35) says weighted minimum values may be more suitable and the lower score should be used instead of the average. The AI RMF has the autonomy stem four times, not three, and one page reference there is wrong. Two Volume I word counts are off, and two paraphrases overstate the source. The SP 800-53 negative hypothesis holds: one occurrence, about human autonomy, in footnote 28. The project website did not answer, and the SP 1011 DOI serves Version 1.0, not 1.1.
